https://www.newstatesman.com/cover-story.text: There was a time when you could reasonably expect a national government to comport itself with marginally more sobriety than an anonymous social media account – the kind that is often adorned with the avatar of an ape. That expectation was touchingly naive. There they were, in all their glory: the governments of Italy, of Finland, of Sweden, nations that have given the world the Renaissance, the concept of functional social democracy, and furniture you assemble yourself. They were now reduced to reacting extempore to videos they had encountered on the internet. These were not intelligence briefings or diplomatic cables or satellite reconnaissance, but the sort of material your uncle might forward at two in the morning with a subject line that’s entirely in capital letters. Incidentally, those who come in on that basis are quite capable of diffusing out of the NHS into other jobs once any conditions expire and indefinite leave to remain is granted, re-creating NHS staff shortages whose filling requires – guess what? – yet more immigration. That’s even more true of the low-paid care sector of course. And if mass immigration were really the route to the sunlit uplands, doesn’t the scale of mass immigration over the last 20 years suggest that Britain should now be a nirvana? – rather than the threadbare and divided place it has become? Blair’s decision to allow Eastern European immigration with no cooling-off post-accession period was one of the most disastrous mistakes made by any politician, and it infuriates me that the Labour party expects me to tramp the streets delivering leaflets trying to drum up support (which I grudgingly do, being a sucker for moral blackmail) when it has lost so much through this gratuitous misjudgement. 0 Reply Jane Saunte 13 days ago “and large portions of its own political elites took the side of the assailant.” Sophistry of the first order. Just because the political elites of Europe blamed Spain for the crisis, does not mean that these same elites supported and took the side of Morocco. 2 Reply David Lawton 13 days ago Reply to Jane Saunte Surely they did so effectively by blaming Spain. This is not sophistry at all. And the wider point – European solidarity collapsed – is spot-on, as is the Greenland warning. 3 Reply Graham Wright 13 days ago Disordered as the response has been from the EU capitals, it is intelligible in that the fear must be of another accretion of support to the insurgent populist parties (even the populist Meloni has this to fear). And perhaps the true cause of the reaction was not the “invasion” of Ceuta, but Spain’s naturalisation initiative. Ultimately, EU elites have to listen to their own national electorates, and lectures de haut en bas never go down too well. 2 Reply Chris 13 days ago Spain’s foolish decision to grant citizenship to those who entered the country illegally before a given (recent) date has inevitably created the expectation that those who migrate illegally now will gain citizenship from some similar amnesty in a few years. We would not encourage benefit or tax fraud like that, so why do it for illegal immigration? And the point of course is that even though we have left the EU and therefore those with new Spanish passports can’t come to Britain as would have been their right before, with the British people debarred by EU ‘Freedom of Movement’ from exercising any democratic control over who comes to our country, they will become part of the more general problem of the influx into Europe from the third world. Bruno Macaes is too focussed on liberal point-scoring to address these realities, and his article is an opportunity wasted. 2 Reply DonS 13 days ago Pope Leo couldn’t have said it better. US Catholic Social Services lost over 3 Billion (yes billion US dollars) tax payer money (Biden) over three years paid for their efforts to lure, house, feed and relocate foreign citizens, in US alone. Rome has been unhappy with the Thump for his lack of charity. The Pope now says he’s on the 60,000 African immigrants into Cueta side. If anyone “ shrieked incoherently and publicly” it’s those like Leo or the US Congress woman Balint from Vermont, the latter on Youtube who said we need migrants to ‘wipe our asses’. I recently volunteered for four semesters teaching English as Second language to a class of Mexican and Mexican Americans. They fear the immigrant invasions more than anyone as it undercuts what little income they have and the taxes they pay for “wiping our asses.” One of their Mexican nephews drove into a tree after a seventeen hour day roofing for cash, and it took months before my class raised enough money to send the body back to Mexico. It is cheap sophistry, or worse, for governments and businesses to lure foreign citizens with someone else’s money to the West for back-breaking labor, cheap sex, ballots or worse, and then drape yourself in charity. The Western media sure makes it all sound so progressive. 2 Reply Jon Stanley 13 days ago It may very be that ‘Uncle’ had it right, and you had it wrong 0 Reply Tony Buck 13 days ago Macaes is one of the leftist imbeciles who have destroyed Europe. He is no position to lecture Europe about anything. 0 Reply wpDiscuz This article appears in the 05 Aug 2026 issue of the New Statesman, Europe's shame Bruno Maçães

Photograph: Sylwester Uchanski/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Poland calls for ‘double’ support to Kyiv after Russian train attack Polish minister denounces ‘escalation’ after strike near border with UK’s Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief David Petraeus nearby. What we know on day 1,664 Guardian staff and agencies Sun 13 Sep 2026 22.23 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Poland and Ukraine have denounced Russian strikes close to the Polish border as an “escalation” in the war after a train was targeted while former British prime minister Boris Johnson and ex-CIA director David Petraeus were at a border station nearby. The escalation should lead to allies to “double” their support for Ukraine, Poland’s foreign minister said in Kyiv. “This was just a few hundred metres from the Polish border, this affects the safety of my countrymen,” Radoslaw Sikorski said. Polish prime minister Donald Tusk chaired an emergency meeting in Warsaw after the strikes, warning he expected Russia to escalate the war “in the coming weeks”. He added: “We cannot exclude that the escalation will also affect our territory … I hope not.” 0:50 Russian drone strike hits train near Poland-Ukraine border – video Poland and Ukraine said the Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train was struck just 2km from the Polish border , reporting no casualties. Shortly beforehand a diplomatic train was at Yagodyn station including Johnson and former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt as well as security advisers from several EU member states, while former CIA director David Petraeus was aboard another train at the station when the attack occurred, the Ukrzaliznytsia rail operator said. It did not say how far the officials were from the train struck. Zelenskyy said Moscow had “deliberately” struck the locomotive . “It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand,” the Ukrainian president said. Ukrainian Railways said Johnson and Petraeus may have been the target, report Amy Hawkins and Charlotte Higgins . Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said the attack was “Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato”. Donald Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks were causing a global shortage. “Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing – he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters in Ireland after diesel prices in the US hit a record high on Friday. “We spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.” Kyiv says Russia’s oil industry funds and fuels Moscow’s war on Ukraine. Trump sought to tie Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries to rising oil prices, saying it was these attacks and not America’s ongoing conflict with Iran that were responsible for price rises . “This isn’t done by the Middle East, this is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine,” the US president said. According to a report published on Friday by the International Energy Agency, net exports of diesel and oil from the Gulf countries in August stood at “just over a quarter” of what they were before the war on Iran began in February. “Disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the agency wrote. The Kremlin said negotiations with Ukraine and the US on the war could take place in October . “We do not rule out such a possibility – we are talking about the foreseeable future,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said, cited by Russia’s Ria and Tass news agencies. Zelenskyy said separately he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami in December, but Peskov said that was “impossible”, repeating Moscow’s demand that a meeting could only take place in the Russian capital. Putin has repeatedly rejected offers for face-to-face talks with the Ukrainian president. Zelenskyy has imposed sanctions on a former press secretary, ⁠accusing her and nine others of spreading Russian propaganda and of supporting Russia’s aggressive policy ⁠towards Ukraine. Yuliia Mendel, who ⁠worked with ​Zelenskyy from 2019 to 2021, before Russia’s invasion – responded with a message on Facebook saying it ⁠was unconstitutional to impose sanctions on Ukrainian citizens. She did not comment on the specific accusations. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27934.text: Big News Network.com Estonia beats Luxembourg to move into second place in Nations League group TALLINN, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Estonia defeated Luxembourg 1-0 at Tallinn's A. Le Coq Arena on Saturday to claim its first victory in the 2026-27 UEFA Nations League and strengthen its position in League C Group 4. The victory lifted Estonia to five points from three matches and moved it into second place in the group, keeping the Baltic side firmly in contention for promotion. Estonia had entered the match unbeaten but without a victory after opening its campaign with a 1-1 draw away to Iceland and a goalless draw in Bulgaria. Luxembourg, meanwhile, had three points from its opening two matches. With three rounds remaining, Estonia's prospects will largely depend on its next match against group leader Iceland in Tallinn on Tuesday. It will then travel to Luxembourg on November 13 before completing the league phase at home against Bulgaria on November 16. The group winner earns direct promotion to League B, while the runner-up enters the promotion play-offs, giving Estonia a realistic opportunity to move up from League C if it can maintain its current form. https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: Complaints about NHS wheelchair provision have soared from eight in 2020/21 to 110 in 2025/26. Photograph: Getty Images View image in fullscreen Complaints about NHS wheelchair provision have soared from eight in 2020/21 to 110 in 2025/26. Photograph: Getty Images NHS Disabled people in England ‘have to wait up to two years for wheelchairs’ Ombudsman’s report says delays have profound consequences and limit users’ ability to lead independent lives Denis Campbell Health policy editor Tue 10 Nov 2026 19.01 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Disabled people are having to wait up to two years to get a wheelchair because of delays involving NHS bodies and private firms that make them. The situation is revealed in a report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsman for England , Paula Sussex, who said hold-ups were having profound consequences and limiting wheelchair users’ ability to lead independent lives. In one case a three-year-old boy with cerebral palsy was unable to start nursery at the same time as his twin brother because he had to wait seven months for a wheelchair. He hurt himself several times when he fell from an adapted buggy his parents were using while they waited. Sussex launched an investigation into NHS wheelchair provision after a sharp rise in complaints – from eight in 2020-21 to 110 in 2025-26. Four out of five relate to the handful of private firms that provide wheelchairs to at least half of all children and adults who need one to help them lead independent lives. Most are about people who need a wheelchair having to wait longer than the supposed 18-week maximum to receive either the device or parts for it. “For people who rely on a wheelchair, delays, unsuitable equipment or poor repairs can affect every part of their life”, said Sussex. “There can be profound consequences, from physical pain and emotional distress to limiting their ability to lead full lives.” Elliot Cruz Gardiyanoglu, now six, was three when he faced a seven-month wait for his wheelchair. That also meant that he was unable access education or specialist therapy. “We were never told there would be such a long wait for the wheelchair,” his mother, Jania Cruz, said. “If we had known we would have explored other ways to get it, especially so that Elliot did not miss out on starting nursery at the same time as his brother. “It was very hard for him to see his brother going to school while he couldn’t.” Rachel Perrin, the director of Newlife, a charity for disabled children, said Elliot’s experience showed how “the wrong wheelchair – or no wheelchair at all – can be dangerous, as well as keeping children and their families trapped at home and leaving them unable to attend school and take part in activities with siblings and friends”. Graham Woolner, a 68-year-old in Bishop’s Stortford who has spinal muscular atrophy, a degenerative condition, has needed a wheelchair for the last 15 years. He was meant to get a new one by August 2023 but it did not arrive until September 2024, and when it did, it failed to work properly. He did not get one in full working order until October 2025, 26 months past the 18-week deadline. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News UK Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox after newsletter promotion ‘I wish I could say I kept my cool’: my maddening experience with the NHS wheelchair service Read more “After a year of waiting, the wheelchair they gave me broke on the first day. I only made it 100 yards before the batteries died,” Woolner said. “The battery issue was never resolved, so I couldn’t go anywhere for a year with any certainty that I would get there and back. “I like to be independent, go into town and take my dogs for a walk. But it got to the point where I wouldn’t go out without my son in case I needed him to push me home. “The wheelchair is effectively my legs. I need it to live my daily life.” Nick Goldup, the chief executive of the Wheelchair Alliance, said the report shone a light on the systemic problems wheelchair users faced. “Getting wheelchair provision right means giving people the freedom to live their lives and to enable them to contribute meaningfully to society,” he said. Sussex highlights a “regulatory gap” in wheelchair services such as assessment, fitting and repair. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency oversees the equipment, but the remit of the Care Quality Commission – the NHS care watchdog – does not cover the services wheelchair users receive because they are not supervised by a health professional. Integrated care boards (ICBs), NHS regional bodies that commission wheelchair services, have “unreliable information” about how many people locally need a wheelchair and are faced with “an uncompetitive wheelchair market” which is dominated by a handful of private providers. Nor are ICBs good at telling each other when they encounter problems with private firms that provide poor services. An NHS spokesperson said:“Long waits for wheelchairs are unacceptable, denying people the independence and quality of life they deserve. “That’s why our wheelchair quality framework, co-produced with wheelchair users, sets a clear expectation that 92% of people receive their equipment within 18 weeks, and requires commissioners to hold regular performance meetings with providers to identify and tackle delays.” Explore more on these topics NHS England Disability Health news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

An Indonesian national has been captured by Ukraine after being recruited by Russia in Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Ukrinform/Shutterstock Ukraine Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment Capture of man from Java follows reports that hundreds are being recruited from the south-east Asian country as Moscow seeks to boost its war effort Kate Lamb Wed 11 Nov 2026 00.33 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 00.35 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation. The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians. According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years. ‘I made the biggest mistake’: the young Yemeni men lured into the Russian army with empty promises Read more The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort. In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia. A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022. This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military. Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.” Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking. Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims. The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said. The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR). It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.
